description:
I am a third-year Computer Science Engineering student 

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, I am working on EarthWave, a project inspired by the Earth Information Jukebox challenge. Our goal is to transform Earth science data into sounds, creating an interactive experience that helps people explore and understand our planet in a new way.

I am passionate about technology and teamwork, and I look forward to developing my skills while contributing to an innovative project.
summary: EarthWave is a web app that lets people listen to Earth science data. We built it for the challenge “The Earth Information Jukebox”. Users pick any location on an interactive map. The app retrieves daily NASA POWER data for that point (temperature, rainfall, wind speed and solar radiation) and shows it with NASA GIBS satellite imagery and charts. It then turns each variable into sound with the Web Audio API. Temperature sets the pitch, rainfall sets the rhythm, wind sets the intensity and sunlight sets the brightness. Users can combine variables and hear how they change together over time. A talking globe and a chart explainer narrate the data in English and French. A Studio mode lets users build their own environmental soundscapes. EarthWave makes Earth data accessible to people who can’t easily read charts, such as visually impaired users, and makes science more engaging for students. It helps people feel climate patterns, not only see them.
details:
How EarthWave Works

EarthWave transforms NASA Earth science data into sound, allowing people to listen to our planet instead of only observing charts and numbers.

In Earth Explorer, users can select any location through an interactive map or search for a city or country. The application retrieves daily NASA POWER data for the selected location, including:

  • Temperature (T2M)
  • Precipitation (PRECTOTCORR)
  • Wind speed (WS2M)
  • Solar radiation (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN)

The application displays this information through interactive charts and NASA GIBS satellite imagery. Its sonification engine, developed with the Web Audio API, translates each environmental variable into a distinct sound:

  • Temperature controls the musical pitch.
  • Rainfall controls the rhythm and intensity of water-drop sounds.
  • Wind is represented by filtered noise.
  • Solar radiation controls the brightness of a background drone.

Users can combine these sounds to explore how different environmental variables interact over time. Missing NASA data is handled as silence rather than being replaced with invented values.

EarthWave Studio provides another way to explore the environment. Users can select soil and rock types and configure atmospheric conditions such as temperature, precipitation, humidity and wind to generate their own virtual environmental soundscapes.

The application also includes a talking globe and a chart explainer that use speech synthesis to explain environmental information in English and French.

Benefits and Intended Impact

EarthWave aims to make Earth science more accessible and engaging.

It offers an alternative way to understand environmental information, particularly for people who have difficulty interpreting traditional charts, including visually impaired users. It can also support teachers and students by making topics such as weather, climate and environmental change more interactive.

Our goal is to help people experience environmental patterns through sound, making scientific data more intuitive and memorable.

Technologies Used
  • HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript
  • Leaflet.js for interactive maps
  • Chart.js for data visualization
  • Web Audio API for sound generation
  • Web Speech API for narration
  • NASA POWER API for environmental data
  • NASA GIBS for satellite imagery
  • Cloudflare Pages for frontend hosting
  • Cloudflare Workers for backend hosting
Creativity and Innovation

EarthWave approaches scientific data from a different perspective by transforming environmental measurements into an interactive sound experience.

Instead of simply displaying numbers, each environmental variable becomes a musical element. Users can listen to individual variables or combine them to discover patterns and relationships.

The Studio mode extends this concept by allowing users to create soundscapes based on geological and atmospheric conditions.

Factors Considered
  • Scientific integrity: Sonification is an educational representation of data, not a recording of real environmental sounds or a physical law.
  • Data reliability: Missing NASA values are handled without inventing measurements.
  • Accessibility: Audio feedback and bilingual narration provide alternative ways to explore information.
  • User experience: Interactive controls, clear visualizations and sound settings make the application easier to use.
  • Responsible communication: EarthWave is an educational project and does not make medical or therapeutic claims.
